source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters, Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity - A meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect (Learning and Instruction 98:102142)
finding: First formal meta-analysis of the effect. Support helps low-prior-knowledge learners and hurts high-prior-knowledge learners, both at medium size. Read through a secondary blog summary only; the paper itself (Elsevier) returned 403 or a redirect.
numbers: 60 studies, 176 effect sizes, almost 6,000 participants. Low prior knowledge: d = 0.505 favouring high support. High prior knowledge: d = -0.428 (low support better).
limits: Numbers come from a blog summary of the paper, not the paper. Pooled CIs, heterogeneity and publication-bias tests not seen. Mostly human lab and classroom studies.
agent_relevance: Best single estimate of size: about half an SD each way. Fading help for strong classes is worth a medium effect, not a huge one, so expect to detect it only with enough items.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters, Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity - A meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect (Learning and Instruction 98:102142) - moderators
finding: Moderators: effect grows with learner age and is strongest in higher education; smaller in language and humanities; few primary-school studies.
numbers: Direction only reported in the summary; no moderator coefficients seen.
limits: Blog summary only. Moderator sizes unverified.
agent_relevance: Expect the reversal to be clearest on structured, rule-based tasks and weaker on open verbal tasks.

source: Kalyuga (2007) Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction (Educ Psychol Rev 19:509-539) - overall effect-size differences
finding: Narrative review with a table of effect sizes for novices and experts in each study. Reversals were found for diagrams plus text, animations, worked examples, hypertext, imagination prompts and more. Author notes full reversals were more often seen in cross-sectional than in longitudinal studies, and that some expert/novice labels rested only on years of schooling.
numbers: More than 2200 students. Conservative effect-size differences (novice d minus expert d) ranged 0.45 to 2.99, mid-range 1.72. Author reads this as about 0.86 each side if symmetric.
quote: The effect has been consistently replicated in many experiments with a large range of instructional materials
limits: Author is the effect's main proponent; no meta-analytic weighting, no bias check; effect sizes recomputed with the larger SD when data were missing. Many cells had N = 10-60. The 2025 meta-analysis (b01) gives smaller values (0.5 and -0.43), so the 2007 table likely overstates the typical size.
agent_relevance: Treat the 2007 table as an upper bound. Use the 2025 pooled values as the planning figure.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler, Sweller (1998) Levels of expertise and instructional design, diagram plus text longitudinal study, as tabulated in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: Same trainees were tested as novices and again after intensive training in electrical wiring. Novices learned best from text embedded in the diagram. After training, diagram-only was better. The same people flipped direction.
numbers: Diagram with embedded text vs diagram only. Operation/troubleshooting test: novices d = 1.67 (N 17), experts d = -0.44 (N 30). Fault-finding test: novices 1.89, experts -0.88. Difference 2.11 and 2.77.
limits: Effect sizes recomputed by Kalyuga 2007, not the original authors. Narrow industrial task, a few weeks of training. Small N.
agent_relevance: Strongest design for our case: the same learner flips. Fading by pass rate mirrors this within a run.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler, Sweller (2000) narrated animated diagrams, as tabulated in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: Narrated explanations with animated diagrams helped novices (modality effect) and became redundant for the same learners after training.
numbers: Novices d = 1.18 (N 30), experts d = -0.62 (N 38), difference 1.80. Diagram-only group outperformed after several training sessions.
limits: Mechanical engineering diagrams; effect sizes derived by the review author.
agent_relevance: Explanations that duplicate what a strong model already knows may cost it attention.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler, Sweller (2001a, 2001b) worked examples vs problem solving or exploration in relay circuit tasks, as tabulated in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: The worked-example advantage vanished as trainees gained experience. In one experiment problem solving beat worked examples for the harder circuits after training. In another, exploratory learning overtook worked examples.
numbers: 2001b Exp 1 programming relay circuits: novices d = 0.90 (N 24), experts 0.23 (N 24). 2001b Exp 2 switching equations: -0.26 vs -0.75 (N 24 each). 2001a Exp 2 worked examples vs exploration: novices 0.69 (N 17), experts -0.33 (N 17).
limits: Several rows are only a partial reversal (expert effect near zero or not significant). The review calls partial reversals the common case.
agent_relevance: Direct support for dropping worked examples from the prompt once the class passes reliably.

source: Tuovinen & Sweller (1999); Kalyuga & Sweller (2004 Exp 3), as tabulated in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: Worked examples beat exploration or problem solving for novices and lost to them for more knowledgeable learners. Cross-sectional designs.
numbers: Tuovinen & Sweller: novices d = 0.91 (N 17), experts -0.31 (N 15). Kalyuga & Sweller 2004 Exp 3: novices 1.20 (N 21), experts -0.36 (N 21).
limits: Group labels came from pre-tests; small N.
agent_relevance: Support for gating by a measured level rather than by a fixed schedule.

source: Reisslein, Atkinson, Seeling, Reisslein (2006) Encountering the expertise reversal effect with a computer-based environment on electrical circuit analysis (Learning and Instruction), as tabulated in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: A different research group replicated the reversal with example-problem pairs vs problem-example pairs and vs faded worked examples, with larger groups (about 60 per cell). The effects were small.
numbers: Example-problem vs problem-example: novices d = 0.33 (N 62), experts -0.37 (N 60). Example-problem vs faded worked examples: novices 0.28 (N 63), experts -0.26 (N 61).
limits: Small effects. Even faded examples (the proposed fix) were worse than example-problem pairs for novices and better for experts, so fading is a trade-off, not a free fix.
agent_relevance: Fading helps experts but costs novices a little. Choose the fade point by evidence, not by default.

source: Reisslein (2005) dissertation on pace of transitioning to problem solving, as tabulated in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: Slow transition from examples to problems helped novices a lot and hurt experts. Pace of fading matters.
numbers: Slow vs fast: novices d = 1.30 (N 39), experts -0.47 (N 44). Slow vs immediate: novices 0.51 (N 38), experts -0.42 (N 45).
limits: Dissertation; not peer reviewed in the form tabulated.
agent_relevance: Fading speed is itself a tunable setting. Slow for weak classes, fast for strong ones.

source: Lee et al. (2006) iconic vs symbolic representations in a gas-law simulation, as tabulated and described in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: Icons helped low-knowledge middle-school students and hurt high-knowledge ones, but only when the material had two parameters at a time. With three parameters at once (high intrinsic load) icons helped everyone.
numbers: Reported difference 2.99, the largest in the review: novices 0.30 (N 48), experts -1.39 (N 63).
limits: Boundary condition: when the task overloads even experts, support helps all. Single study.
agent_relevance: Do not fade help on tasks that are hard for the whole class. Fade only when the task fits current ability.

source: Leahy & Sweller (2005) Interactions among the imagination, expertise reversal, and element interactivity effects (J Exp Psychol Appl); Ginns et al. (2003), as described in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: The reversal depends on element interactivity. Leahy and Sweller used the same children as novices and, two weeks later, as relative experts on bus timetables and temperature graphs; study beat imagining for novices and the reverse held for experts. A larger spread in element interactivity gave stronger effects.
numbers: Leahy & Sweller experts' effect sizes: Exp 1 -0.37 and -0.80 (N 30 per cell); Exp 2 -0.45 and -0.79. Ginns et al. (2003) imagining vs studying, transfer scores: novices 0.55, experts -1.14.
limits: Primary-school tasks. Element-interactivity split was by materials chosen by authors.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that task complexity and learner knowledge together decide whether help is redundant.

source: Kalyuga & Sweller (2004, 2005); Kalyuga (2006a); Salden et al. (2006); Corbalan et al. (2006), adaptive tutoring from rapid tests, as described in Kalyuga (2007)
finding: Fixing the fix: choosing the guidance level dynamically from a short first-step test (and later an efficiency measure combining score and rated effort) beat non-adapted instruction.
numbers: Kalyuga & Sweller 2004: knowledge gain effect size 0.46. 2005: knowledge gain 0.55, efficiency gain 0.69. Salden et al. (2006) personalised task selection: 0.58. Corbalan et al. (2006) shared control: posttest 0.25, lower load 0.37.
limits: Small and medium effects; domains narrow (algebra, kinematics, air-traffic control, dietetics). The two adaptation procedures did not differ from each other.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S0: measure state (pass rate plus effort), then choose the guidance level. Cheap rapid tests worked as well as heavier models.

source: Tobias (2009) The expertise reversal effect and aptitude treatment interaction research (Commentary); Schnotz (2009) Reanalyzing the expertise reversal effect (both Instructional Science)
finding: Two commentaries in the same journal issue. Tobias links the effect to older aptitude-treatment-interaction research. Schnotz re-analyses it. Only titles and authors confirmed through Crossref; text not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Unopened. Pointers for the rival-explanation thread.
agent_relevance: Follow up: ATI history suggests the effect may be less stable than the reversal label suggests.

source: Rey & Buchwald (2011) The expertise reversal effect: Cognitive load and motivational explanations (J Exp Psychol Appl)
finding: Title indicates a motivational rival to the cognitive-load explanation. Only title and authors confirmed via Crossref and Europe PMC; text not read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Unopened. Rival-explanation thread.
agent_relevance: If part of the effect is motivation, an LLM (no boredom) may show less of it.

source: Rey & Fischer (2013) The expertise reversal effect concerning instructional explanations (Instructional Science 41)
finding: Reversal tested for instructional explanations, a close analogue of text hints. Only title confirmed; text not read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Hints and explanations are the most prompt-like form of support; read this next.

source: Chen, Kalyuga, Sweller (2017) The expertise reversal effect is a variant of the more general element interactivity effect (Educ Psychol Rev)
finding: Rival framing: the reversal is one case of element interactivity. Repository page returned 403; only the title and the way a citing paper (Gorbunova 2025) uses it were seen. SUBFIELDS.md dates it 2016; the citing paper gives 2017.
numbers: None read.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable rule: help matters in proportion to task element interactivity, not only to learner level.

source: Gorbunova, Kapuza, Chen, Costley (2025) Rethinking pre-training: cognitive load implications for learners with varying prior knowledge (Front Psychol 16:1628047)
finding: A study that did not find the expected reversal. Concept map plus glossary pre-training lowered extraneous load for everyone, including high-prior-knowledge learners. High-knowledge learners also had lower intrinsic and extraneous load and higher germane load.
numbers: N = 136 graduate students, median split on prior knowledge, 2x2 mixed ANOVA; power analysis assumed eta-squared 0.06 (n = 125 needed). Problem-solving score table: overall mean 7.51 of 13.5 max (SD 2.43).
limits: Median split; self-reported load scales; one online session; one university. Support was short and cheap, so little redundancy cost was possible.
agent_relevance: Cheap, short support did not hurt strong learners. Reversal may need support that is long or must be cross-checked against knowledge.

source: Gorbunova et al. (2025) method note and citing of Jung et al. (2024)
finding: Power details needed to judge how strong the null is. The authors based power on a 2024 programming pre-training study reporting eta-squared 0.06 to 0.09; the sample met the 125 needed for an interaction of that size.
numbers: Alpha 0.05, power 0.80, Cohen's f 0.25; N = 136, 73.6% women, over 15 programmes at one university.
limits: Homogeneous sample and median split reduce power for an interaction; a null here is weak evidence against the effect.
agent_relevance: Small designs rarely test the interaction well. Do not read single nulls as refutation.

source: Seufert (2019) Training for coherence formation when learning from text and picture and the interplay with learners' prior knowledge (Front Psychol 10:193)
finding: The opposite pattern. Strategy training helped only learners with high prior knowledge; low-knowledge learners got no benefit. This is an aptitude-treatment interaction where help needs knowledge to use, not a reversal.
numbers: N = 30. Prior knowledge x training interaction for recall beta = 0.42, p = 0.04. Prior-knowledge slope in trained group beta = 0.81, p = 0.001; in control beta = 0.19, p = 0.31. Comprehension: slope 0.73, p = 0.003 vs 0.15 n.s.; training had no overall effect (beta 0.08, p = 0.61).
limits: Very small N, regression on one sample, three-week training.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: help that is a procedure to run can need a knowledge base. Weak models may not execute a strategy prompt well.

source: Tang et al. (2026) AI-driven adaptive training for utility employees: a three-wave cluster-randomized field experiment (Front Psychol 17:1944626)
finding: Large field test of knowledge-graph-driven adaptive training vs uniform training. Adaptive helped a little overall and helped more experienced employees more, opposite to the compensatory (novices gain more) pattern. Authors say this fits the expertise-reversal account because uniform training forces redundant material on experienced workers.
numbers: Analysed N = 2,574 of 3,000 invited, six power-company sites. Knowledge d about 0.29 at T2 and 0.26 at 6-week follow-up; self-efficacy d 0.26; transfer intention d 0.25. Extraneous load d = -0.34, intrinsic load d = +0.28. Condition x tenure interaction b = 0.032 per year, p < 0.001; baseline tenure imbalance d = 0.08.
limits: Not a clean test: arms differ in delivery medium as well as adaptivity; tenure moderation was exploratory; the system is knowledge-graph-driven, not an LLM; workplace, not classroom.
agent_relevance: Adaptive routing paid off more for experienced learners, so saving by skipping redundant material was real. Gains from adaptivity were small (d 0.25-0.29).

source: Authors not recorded (2025) Who regulates? Effects of scaffolding in system- and self-regulated learning (Front Psychol 16:1543024)
finding: Scaffolding improved recall and self-efficacy. Prior knowledge moderated the effect only for comprehension, and only in a three-way interaction with who regulates the path. No main effect of system vs self regulation.
numbers: N = 102 students, 2x2 design. Comprehension model R2 = 14.27%, F(7, 94) = 2.236, p = 0.038; three-way interaction R2 change 4.36%, F(1, 94) = 4.781, p = 0.031. Transfer and recall moderation hypotheses rejected.
limits: Moderation on one of three outcomes; many tests; PROCESS model 3; the paper has a correction notice.
agent_relevance: Prior-knowledge moderation shows up inconsistently across outcomes. Test fading on each outcome.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2409.12183)
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models. A reasoning scaffold in the prompt helps only on symbolic tasks; elsewhere the gain is tiny.
numbers: Average CoT gain 14.2 (symbolic), 12.3 (math), 6.9 (logic). Top three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1. As much as 95% of the MMLU gain came from questions with an equals sign.
limits: Not a test of fading by model strength; models differ.
agent_relevance: Support is task-dependent for LLMs too. Match the scaffold to the task type before fading by model strength.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (arXiv 2410.21333 v4, June 2025)
finding: Six tasks from psychology where deliberation hurts people. In three, models got much worse with CoT; in others the effect was mixed. Support can hurt LLMs for reasons that mirror human results.
numbers: Up to 36.3% absolute accuracy drop for OpenAI o1-preview compared to GPT-4o in the worst task; three of six tasks showed significant drops.
limits: Not an expertise manipulation. Tasks were chosen from human results.
agent_relevance: Direct warning: an added reasoning scaffold can cut accuracy. Keep an unscaffolded arm for every state.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models (arXiv 2201.11903)
finding: The other end of the scale: CoT hurts small models. Models below about 100B parameters produced fluent but illogical chains, scoring below standard prompting. Help can hurt the weakest as well as the strongest.
numbers: Gains appear only at about 100B parameters and above. PaLM 540B with 8 exemplars set the state of the art on GSM8K at the time.
limits: 2022 models; the scale cut-off has probably moved.
agent_relevance: The LLM version is a hump, not a one-way slope: too weak to use the help, too strong to need it. Fade by measured pass rate per class, not assumed strength.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: incentivizing reasoning capability in LLMs via reinforcement learning (arXiv 2501.12948)
finding: A model-side reversal in practice: for the trained reasoning model, few-shot examples consistently lowered performance, and the authors recommend a zero-shot prompt that only states the problem and the output format.
numbers: No numbers given for the drop. Several few-shot benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, C-Eval, CLUE-WSC) were switched to zero-shot for evaluation.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: Vendor statement without a visible ablation table; model-specific.
agent_relevance: Most direct LLM evidence: strong reasoners do worse with demonstrations. Fade examples out of the S0 prompt for strong classes.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (arXiv 2302.00093)
finding: Adding irrelevant information dramatically lowers LLM accuracy. Extra text has a cost to models as it does to people (the redundancy mechanism behind the reversal).
numbers: GSM-IC benchmark. Mitigations: self-consistency and an instruction to ignore irrelevant context. No single headline figure read.
limits: Distractor sentences, not redundant help.
agent_relevance: Supports the mechanism: extra text costs the model something. Keep S0 help short.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) bibliographic record from Crossref
finding: Confirms authors (Leonard Tetzlaff, Bianca Simonsmeier, Tabea Peters, Garvin Brod) and venue (Learning and Instruction, article 102142). No abstract in the record.
numbers: None.
limits: Paper behind a login; numbers in b01 are from a blog.
agent_relevance: Open the paper when access is possible to confirm CIs and bias tests.

source: AI-assisted comparative exercise vs conventional labeling in ophthalmic anatomy (Front Med 2026, authors not recorded)
finding: Quasi-experiment using Gemini 3.0 Pro to make anatomy variants. No knowledge difference between AI and conventional exercise. Satisfaction and self-rated gains appeared in non-medical (novice) students but not in medical students, a mild reversal-like pattern.
numbers: N = 121 sophomores in two Shanghai universities. Non-medical students: satisfaction 9.17 vs 7.52, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001, r = 0.60; self-assessed performance 7.76 vs 6.03, p = 0.003, r = 0.47. Knowledge post-test p > 0.05 throughout.
limits: Intact classes, not random; self-report outcomes; the LLM made the stimuli, it did not tutor. No knowledge effect.
agent_relevance: LLM-made support fits the novice-expert split in satisfaction but did not change knowledge.

source: Exploring the effect of GenAI on learning outcomes in higher education: a three-level meta-analysis (Front Psychol 2026)
finding: Meta-analysis of generative AI in education. Overall medium effect; teaching method was the only significant moderator; other moderators had no significant influence.
numbers: 36 studies, 132 effect sizes, 7,229 participants. Overall g = 0.499. Collaborative learning g = 1.026; blended learning g = 0.633; higher-order learning g = 0.504.
limits: Not about expertise reversal. Seven moderators tested; prior knowledge was not reported as a moderator in the abstract.
agent_relevance: GenAI help in education has a medium average effect, but no learner-level moderator was found significant in this study.

source: Search note: Europe PMC for 'expertise reversal' 2023-2026 hits
finding: Open-database search found no registered replication or Many Labs style replication of the reversal. The evidence base is the Sweller/Kalyuga group's studies, a 2025 meta-analysis, and scattered new field tests (sport tactics, language, medical education). Recent tests include an imagination reversal in basketball tactics (2024) and a pen-tablet study with emotions (2023), unread.
numbers: Zero registered replications found in this index.
limits: Absence of evidence from an incomplete index. The WebSearch quota was exhausted and OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv search APIs were rate limited, so the search was narrow.
agent_relevance: Treat the effect as likely real, medium, and context dependent.
